newsitem.title: USA: Fleming says being sued by Furr's.
newsitem.headline: Fleming says being sued by Furr's.

text.p: Fleming Companies Inc said Friday that on February 28 Furr's Supermarkets of Albuquerque, New Mexico, filed a lawsuit against Fleming claiming Furr's was overcharged for products under its supply agreement with Fleming.
The suit alleges breach of contract, misrepresentation, fraud and violation of certain of New Mexico's trade practice statutes, Fleming said.
Furr's seeks a declaratory judgment terminating the supply agreement, along with an unspecified monetary award, including punitive and treble damages, Fleming said.
The company said it believes it complied with its obligations to Furr's in all material respects, and in good faith.
As a 35 percent owner of Furr's, Fleming has an obvious commitment to their success, the company said.

Fleming said an unfavorable outcome or the loss of Furr's business, neither of which the company foresees, could have a material adverse effect on the company. "We intend to vigorously defend Fleming against the lawsuit," the company said.
Furr's, Fleming's largest customer, purchased $546 million of products in 1996, under a 10-year supply agreement expiring in 2001, Fleming said.
Fleming said it supplies goods and services to some of its customers (particularly larger ones) pursuant to supply agreements containing a "competitiveness" clause.
Under this clause, Fleming said, a customer may submit a qualified bid from another supplier to provide a comparable range of goods at prices lower than those charged by Fleming.
In order to qualify as "competitive," the bid must be lower than Fleming's prices by more than a stated percentage, Fleming said.

Upon finding a qualified bid, Fleming said it has the right to lower its prices and come within the agreed percentage of the competitor's bid; if Fleming chooses not to lower prices, the customer may accept the competitor's bid.
The competitiveness clause is not exercised frequently and disputes regarding the clause must generally be submitted to binding arbitration, Fleming said.
Additionally, most supply agreements prohibit recovery of both consequential and punitive damages, Fleming said.
Recently, Furr's has been seeking to exercise the competitiveness clause of its supply agreement, Fleming said.
Fleming said "with Fleming's cooperation, Furr's has been examining the pricing under our supply agreement."
This week, Fleming said, Furr's submitted a bid by a potential competitor to supply Furr's approximately 70 stores in New Mexico and West Texas.
Fleming said it is examining the submission, but said it has not yet determined whether it is qualified or competitive.
Fleming Companies Inc distributes food and related products, and offers retail services, to more than 3,100 supermarkets in 42 states, which includes approximately 270 company-owned stores.
The suit was filed in the Second Judicial District Court, County of Bernalillo, New Mexico. No hearings have been scheduled yet, a spokesman for Furr's said.

"We're making it clear to Fleming that we're available to try to settle this out of court," Patrick Totman, Furr's chief financial officer told Reuters in a telephone interview. "Failing settlement, we are absolutely resolved to pursue this lawsuit to conclusion."
